title: Stability play notes: graduated recovery & backoff snapshot
content:
Purpose
This note sketches a graduated recovery play and operator checklist focused on common API degradation modes we keep seeing: hard timeouts, large-batch-induced tail latency, 429 storms, degraded streaming (partial frames/EOFs), and elevated 5xx/error rates. Aim: pragmatic, fast mitigations to restore customer-facing success while preserving telemetry for postmortem.

Status/context
- Draft: distilled from recent oncall runs in Q4 2025 and a pair of postmortem sessions.
- Not a formal runbook yet; intended as a compact operator-friendly reference to use during incidents and to iterate into a formal playbook.

Quick TL;DR recovery ladder (apply top->down until healthy):
1) Feature-gate nonessential workloads (burst/backfill) -> throttle by tag.
2) Fail fast lower-cost routes: enable fallback routing to stateless smaller model variant or cached-response path.
3) Reduce per-request resource pressure: limit max_tokens / reduce batch size / lower concurrency cap per-worker.
4) Route to warm standby region or Dedicated capacity (if configured).
5) Short rolling restarts of worker pool / recycle long-running kernels.
6) Escalate to infra (GPU host) for node-level restarts or capacity expansion.

Observability pointers (quick queries)
- High-level signals: 99th percentile latency, 95th latency, error-rate %, QPS per route, request queue depth.
- PromQL snippets to paste quickly into pager:
  - 95p latency for /v1/generate: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/v1/generate"}[2m])) by (le))
  - 429 rate by model: sum(rate(http_responses_total{code="429"}[1m])) by (model)
  - queue depth per worker type: sum(workqueue_depth{pool=~".*gpu.*"}) by (pool)
- Kibana dashboards to open: "API Latency Overview", "Model Worker Health", "Streaming Frame Loss".

Triage checklist (first 8 minutes)
- Confirm scope: sample failing request ids from logger (search trace_id pattern) -> are failures global or tied to a model/region/customer?
- Check short-term telemetry: sudden spike in 5xx or 429, concurrent rise in request queue depth, GPU utilization anomalies.
- If 429s dominant: check rate-limit changes or new traffic sources (recent deploys / traffic shift).
- If streaming degraded: inspect partial-frame logs and proxy timeouts.
- Run simple smoke: curl the health endpoint of the gateway and a small generation against fallback model (10 tokens).

Mitigations by failure mode
1) Timeouts / elevated tail latency
  - Symptoms: p95/p99 jump, request queue depth growing, some requests hang and exceed runtime timeouts.
  - Immediate mitigations:
    * Toggle aggressive request preemption: limit per-request compute time to X ms (operator knob).
    * Decrease max_tokens default at gateway for affected routes.
    * Lower batch size on serving pool for short window (decreases latency at cost of throughput).
    * Activate prefix/KV cache hot-path bypass if cache thrash seen.
  - If persists after 10m: schedule rolling restart of selected worker group, prioritize warm kernels first.

2) 429 storms (rate limit saturation or upstream throttling)
  - Symptoms: spike in 429s across customers or concentrated on single key; clients see retries.
  - Immediate mitigations:
    * Engage API gateway: raise short-term quota for SRE-run emergency tag OR enable emergency soft-limit (10% time-limited bump).
    * Identify and throttle noisy API keys via token-level rate-limit config.
    * Apply exponential backoff headers for proxied clients if supported.
    * If caused by an internal backfill job: pause job; move to Dedicated pool or schedule smaller batches.
  - Longer actions: carve out a dedicated route for heavy-traffic customers and pin to dedicated capacity.

3) Degraded streaming (partial frames / EOF mid-stream)
  - Symptoms: client reconnects, incomplete JSON frames, high error rate only on streaming endpoints.
  - Immediate mitigations:
    * Bump proxy streaming read timeout for affected route by small delta (+2s) while investigating.
    * Route streaming traffic away from overloaded worker pool (route policy to model variant with less memory pressure).
    * Toggle conservative chunking: server emits shorter frames more frequently to avoid kernel stalls.
  - Check GPU/kernel logs for OOM or kernel stalls and GC events.

4) Elevated error rates (5xx)
  - Symptoms: broad 5xx increase, or model-specific 500/502/503.
  - Immediate mitigations:
    * Circuit-break: add 5xx threshold for automatic short-circuit to fallback model for new requests.
    * Disable nonessential plugins/middleware (sanitizers/validators) that may be failing.
    * If there's a recent deploy flagged in linked_artifacts, rollback that deployment.

Operational knobs (what you can flip quickly)
- API gateway: per-key throttle, emergency quota bump, route-level max_tokens, global request timeout.
- Serving runtime: max_batch_size, concurrency_per_worker, preemption_timeout_ms, kernel-restart flag, cache-eviction-policy.
- Routing: enable-fallback-route, region-failover, pick-model-variant.
- Infra: scale worker pool replicas (auto-scale override), add temporary Dedicated nodes.

Playbook recipes (copyable short sequences)
- 2-minute hotfix for 429 flood:
  1) Identify top 10 tokens by 429 volume (Kibana table).
  2) Apply per-key throttle to top 3 offenders (30s window).
  3) Raise emergency quota for admin/internal keys to let operator tooling through.
  4) Monitor 1m 429 rate; if not falling, block offending key and notify product.

- 10-minute latency containment:
  1) Lower max_batch_size from 64->16 on target pool.
  2) Decrease default max_tokens for affected route by 50%.
  3) Enable fallback-route to a smaller model with same API surface.
  4) Roll restart 10% of pool to reclaim stuck kernels.

Escalation map
- SRE operator (oncall) - first response & temporary remediation (knobs above).
- Runtime/infra engineer - if node-level resource anomaly or kernel hangs detected.
- Product/solutions - when customer-facing SLA is breached or long-term capacity changes required.

Post-incident capture checklist
- Save key query snapshots and link S3 export of logs and traces (prefix: incidents/YYYYMMDD-<short>).
- Mark root-cause hypothesis and supporting evidence in the incident doc.
- List config changes made during incident (knobs + timestamps).
- Action items: quantifiable work with owners and due dates (e.g., implement rate-limit per-customer by 2026-03-01).

Open questions / experiments to run (notes to self)
- Can we automate the 2-minute hotfix for 429s into a playbook that suggests offending keys and one-click throttle?
- Should fallback routes preserve request-level metadata for SLO accounting? (tradeoff: complexity vs transparency)
- Experiment: short-window aggressive preemption vs batch-size reduction — which degrades throughput less at p99? Plan A/B test on a low-risk route.

Appendix: quick commands
- sample health curl: curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_KEY" https://gateway.redwood.ai/_health | jq .
- small smoke generate: curl -sS -X POST https://gateway.redwood.ai/v1/generate -d '{"model":"fallback-alpha","input":"test","max_tokens":8}' -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_KEY"

Notes / meta
- Keep this short, operator-first. Move to canonical runbook after 2 successful uses in incidents.
- If you borrow a mitigation into the canonical runbook, prefer the conservative knob-first approach (throttle/route) before infra restarts.

Unresolved: tenant-specific throttles for PLG keys — product input required before we auto-block.

End of note
